question: Why do nurses write patient notes in the hospital chart?
explanation: You've got this! Documentation helps every shift and team member stay on the same page so the patient gets smooth, continuous care. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h1)

question: When a nurse checks and records a patient's temperature and pulse, which step of the nursing process are they doing?
explanation: Spot on! Checking vital signs is part of gathering information, which is the assessment phase. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h1)

question: If a case goes to court, how is a patient's medical record officially viewed?
explanation: Well done! In court, the patient's chart stands as legal proof of the care that was given. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h2)

question: Why do hospital managers check patient records during quality reviews?

options.A: To evaluate adherence to clinical standards
options.B: To increase patient discharge turnover speed
options.C: To replace routine bedside nursing assessments
options.D: To punish nurses who make slow entries

explanation: Great thinking! These reviews help the hospital see if care matches standard guidelines so everyone stays safe. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h2)

question: In the eyes of the law, what happens if a nurse forgets to write down that they gave a medication?

options.A: The hospital automatically waives all liability
options.B: The pharmacist takes the blame for the omission
options.C: The law assumes the medication was not given
options.D: The patient must pay an extra prescription fee

explanation: Remember: if it isn't documented, legally it didn't happen! Always write down your care promptly. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h3)

question: Which of these actions breaks the rules of patient confidentiality and digital safety?

options.A: Sharing your computer password with a colleague
options.B: Adding late entries with correct timestamps
options.C: Locking the electronic screen when leaving a desk

explanation: Never share your password! It keeps patient files secure and ensures accountability for who views them. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h3)

question: Which of these nursing notes is written as a clear, factual observation?

options.A: Patient had a very restless and uncomfortable night
options.B: Wound is 4 cm long with moderate serosanguinous drainage
options.C: Doctor visited the ward and sorted out the patient
options.D: Patient is uncooperative and complaining about everything

explanation: Awesome! Sticking to measurable facts like size and drainage avoids personal bias in the notes. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h4)

question: Why is it best to write your nursing notes right after doing a procedure?

options.A: It speeds up the process of patient bed allocation
options.B: It removes the need for verbal shift handovers entirely
options.C: It prevents dangerous gaps and forgotten details in memory
options.D: It satisfies hospital marketing department requirements

explanation: Spot on! Writing things down immediately stops us from forgetting crucial details later. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h4)

question: What is the main idea behind Charting by Exception (CBE)?

options.A: Using paper records exclusively without digital backups
options.B: Documenting only abnormal findings or deviations from norms
options.C: Requiring doctors to write all nursing progress notes
options.D: Banning the use of flow sheets and graphic charts

explanation: You've got this! CBE assumes normal care is done, so you only write down when something unusual happens. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h5)

question: How do Problem-Oriented Medical Records (POMR) work differently from older styles of charting?

options.A: All disciplines contribute to a centralized problem list
options.B: Patient complaints are ignored in favor of lab results
options.C: Only doctors are allowed to access the patient file
options.D: Nurses are barred from writing clinical progress notes

explanation: Brilliant! POMR brings doctors, nurses, and other health workers together to focus on one shared list of patient problems. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h5)

question: What does the letter 'S' stand for in the ISBAR communication tool?
explanation: The first 'S' in ISBAR stands for Situation, briefly stating what is happening right now. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h6)

question: Why do nurses prefer structured handovers like ISBAR over casual chatting?

options.A: They eliminate the need to review patient charts
options.B: They reduce the risk of omitting vital clinical details
options.C: They prevent patients from asking questions about care
options.D: They allow nursing shifts to finish in under ten minutes

explanation: Exactly! A structured format makes sure no important safety details get left out during shift change. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h6)

question: Where should a nurse record that an incident report was filled out for a patient who fell?

options.A: In the nursing progress notes of the patient chart
options.B: On the front cover of the bedside clinical file
options.C: On the separate hospital incident report form only
options.D: In the personal diary of the ward unit manager

explanation: Good to know! Incident reports are kept separate from the main patient chart for quality review purposes. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of using incident reports in a hospital?

options.A: Creating legal grounds to dismiss negligent staff
options.C: Identifying systemic flaws to prevent future accidents
options.D: Increasing insurance payouts for hospital damages

explanation: Well done! Incident reports are about finding where the system broke down so we can fix it and protect patients next time. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h7)

question: How should a nurse fix a mistake made while writing in a paper patient chart?

options.A: Draw a single line through the error, write 'error', and initial it
options.B: Apply liquid paper correction fluid over the mistake and rewrite
options.C: Tear out the entire page and rewrite the complete shift notes
options.D: Scratch out the incorrect text heavily until it is unreadable

explanation: Spot on! A neat single strikethrough keeps the record honest and clear while showing a correction was made. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h8)

question: Which of these charting habits is a serious legal and professional mistake?

options.A: Charting medication administration before giving it
options.B: Signing clinical entries with full name and professional rank
options.C: Writing patient progress notes immediately after care
options.D: Using standardized abbreviations approved by the hospital

explanation: Never pre-chart! Recording care before you actually do it is falsifying records and puts patient safety at risk. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T4#GNS112_U3_T4_h8)
